content: Poking around in this repo, I found https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool/tree/main/LeanPool/BrauerGroupNew which just seems to be a copy of some work that one of my PhD students is doing, with no obvious attribution (although you can see their name mentioned in some of the files). Did you ask them if it was OK to (steal/copy/whatever word you want to use for this) their work?

IANAL but, since BrauerGroup ia distributed under Apache License, Vasily has done this right:

  1. Existing copyrig notices are preserved
  2. Modified files are shown to have been modified (no file was modified)
The only thin that's missing is a NOTICE file stating that these files are distributed under the terms of Apache 2.0

Ahem, forgive me for indulging my common sense, but shouldn't there be some explicit attribution "these file were copied from here and there"? (This is not a legal argument... as so often, legal requirements are more of a necessary than a suficient condition.)

Based on my previous experience with repository version upgrades, ensuring that the code compiles post-upgrade is usually not an issue. However, it is very difficult to maintain the original code style; upgrading many of the theorems essentially amounts to re-proving them from scratch.

My question is: how do you ensure that the style of the LLM-generated code does not undergo drastic changes?
A message was moved here from #Project announcements > Lean Pool -- arXiv-like Lean library by Bryan Gin-ge Chen.

Suppose an author finds their work listed under candidates and does not want their work to be copied and maintained by an LLM, what's the process to opt out?

It's probably not a very nice feeling to find one's work on the list without consenting to it (though I wouldn't expect LLMs to understand such human feelings)
I think keeping a sorry in your project might help, so the automated checks think that it is not finished yet. Ideally a wrong sorry, so their agent armada can't fill it in automatically.

@Christian Merten No, that's ridiculous. My point is "why is it opt-in by default". The lean-pool project goes against open source values in that it creates a nonconsensual fork, and continues developing it without contributing back. Am I the only one that feels this way?
Just to say that one of my repos is in this pool, but I was asked if I wanted to have my work be a part of this, which I have no problem with. But it sounds like this was not the case for everyone?
One of my repos was "copied" and I was certainly not asked.

Legally, they have the right to do so, my repo is under Apache 2 (and even if it was under a strong copyleft license, everything would be fine since the pool is open source). Of course, the question about whether this is "respectful behaviour" is a completely different one.

My repo did not have the Apache 2 licence and I was told that if I was indeed happy to have my work in the pool that it would need to have this, which I did add. So that maybe explains why I got asked and you (and others) didn't

We will need to have a "no-index" analog for repositories indicating that they should not be included. Of course, nothing prevents people from ignoring this tag, just as search engines may freely ignore the "no-index" tags.

Niklas Halonen said:

It's probably not a very nice feeling to find one's work on the list without consenting to it (though I wouldn't expect LLMs to understand such human feelings)

Frankly, I was pretty happy to see my formalSnarksProject repo listed there, even though I didn't give direct permission as far as I recall. I put an open source license on that project exactly because I wanted it to be usable by other projects without needing my permission.
Sorry for not responding for a couple days. I am defending my PhD tomorrow so it's a busy time for me.

@Kevin Buzzard , each project has attribution. For example BrouerGroupNew's project card is at https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool/blob/main/LeanPool/BrauerGroupNew.lean#L42-L47. The DOI is wrong though, I think something got messed up with the underscores, since the correct DOI is 10.1007/978-3-031-64529-7_9.

I did not reach out to anyone whose project already had an Apache-2 or MIT license (I did reach out to ~30 people whose project lacked a license asking to add one, and almost everyone added one and approved for their project to be in Lean Pool; only one person declined). If anyone wants their project removed from Lean Pool, they can just ask me here or on GitHub. If you or your student (is it @Yaël Dillies ?) wants their project removed, just let me know!

shouldn't there be some explicit attribution "these file were copied from here and there"

@Michael Rothgang , yes, each project has a project card. They are all in projects.yml. Here is the project card for BrauerGroupNew: https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool/blob/main/LeanPool/projects.yml#L1680-L1727. In fact, this is one of the things the linters enforce! Although the DOI does not resolve, sorry about it, I'll fix it.

how do you ensure that the style of the LLM-generated code does not undergo drastic changes?

@Yi.Yuan , I only ensure that the statements and definitions did not change (unless the bump required a change, which is rare, and usually cosmetic, like how v4.31 disallows underscores in names). The proofs indeed undergo big changes, but I would argue proofs are less important than definitions and statements.

Vasily Ilin said:

your student (is it @Yaël Dillies ?)

No, it is @Edison Xie instead

@Niklas Halonen , which of your projects would you like to be removed from Lean Pool or not added to Lean Pool in the future? Just lmk and I'll remove it.

The whole point of licenses like Apache-2 and MIT is that anyone can take the code and do whatever with it. But I don't want to offend people, so I am happy to remove whatever projects people don't want to have in Lean Pool.

By the way, one of my main criteria for the choosing the ~60 projects to Lean Pool that already got pooled was inactivity. I specifically looked at the last commit and the Lean version. That's because if someone has finished their project, and is not bumping the Lean version, might appreciate someone else bumping their project, as part of Lean Pool.

why is it opt-in by default

Because Apache-2 is an open license.
@Christian Merten , which project is it? Would you like me to remove it?

My repo did not have the Apache 2 licence... So that maybe explains why I got asked and you (and others) didn't

Correct. I did not want to spam everyone. When someone adds Apache-2, they explicitly say to the world "I give permission to do whatever you want with this code". But I am not an adversary and do not want to offend people, so I'll happily remove whatever projects people don't want to see in Lean Pool.
Regarding BrauerGroup specifically, are you saying you bumped it to v4.31? (:tada:)
If so, please contribute back the changes, as we have been struggling with bumping for all these months (eg Whysoserioushah/BrauerGroup#21 is the current place we're stuck on)

are you saying you bumped it to v4.31?

yes. Lean Pool is at v4.31, and BrauerGroup is in Lean Pool. All Lean Pool projects were originally at v4.28 or lower (some were even lower than v4.20!). Bumping them took some work but the agents don't get tired!
But I don't guarantee correctness, let alone code quality! This is very much a prototype I am working on, mostly by myself. I don't have the bandwidth to hand-check each project, I am sorry for that
It's okay, I can cherry-pick the changes I need
The best I can do is ask Claude to make a PR to your repo with the bump. Would you like me to do this, @Yaël Dillies ?
Sure, let's try!
I would like bumps to intermediate versions too, so I might not merge your PR right away

The only thin that's missing is a NOTICE file stating that these files are distributed under the terms of Apache 2.0

@Yaël Dillies , There is a NOTICE file: https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool/blob/main/NOTICE.

I think you might still technically be in trouble for stripping out the original NOTICE/LICENSE/README.md file from the source repositories, especially if they are apache_license ++ extra_licenses or similar, or if the readme contains important attribution.
(but this isn't to say that you can't put the projects there, only that I think you have some extra 'i's to dot and 't's to cross)

Vasily Ilin said:

shouldn't there be some explicit attribution "these file were copied from here and there"

Michael Rothgang , yes, each project has a project card. They are all in projects.yml. Here is the project card for BrauerGroupNew: https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool/blob/main/LeanPool/projects.yml#L1680-L1727. In fact, this is one of the things the linters enforce! Although the DOI does not resolve, sorry about it, I'll fix it.

I see. This projects file is not mentioned anywhere; can you state clearly in the README where these projects are taken from and how to opt out?

(I do think an opt in model would have been nicer, and don't quite see the damage of that. In any case, having no documented opt out at all is really not great. It's not apparent from plain sight that "just write to me" will suffice, imho the AI space has too many different norms to make that a natural assumption.)

For me, part of the damage of an opt-in process is that the view of one project maintainer that gets the opt-in request message might not be the same as other contributors'.

Suppose individual A wants to use a theorem you or I contributed in our work in mathlib. But A decides they should ask permission from some other individual B in the project (maybe the person listed as the copyright holder of the file where the theorem was added, or someone on the maintainer team). Suppose that B decides they didn't like that particular proposed use of mathlib and asks A not to import it in their project, so they don't.

I would be pretty distraught if that happened to me! I would see it as a destruction of the value of my work, and a betrayal to my participation in the mathlib community, which is partially predicated on the open source license we all agreed would apply to our code when we submitted it for review.
@Yaël Dillies , here is the bump PR, from Claude: https://github.com/Whysoserioushah/BrauerGroup/pull/22

This projects file is not mentioned anywhere

@Michael Rothgang , this is not true. It is mentioned in CONTRIBUTING: https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#submitting-a-project, which is the natural place to mention it.

I just added an Opt Out section: https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#opt-out.

I want to point out that Apache-2 already is Opt-in. Adding this or another permissive license is exactly giving permission to other people to use the code in whatever way they want (with attribution).
Of course, I am not an adversary, and will remove whatever projects people request to be removed.

I think this argument is pure bad faith. All those licences were created before the genAI disaster and nobody could have imagined this. And now it’s too late for many projects. For instance changing the licence of Mathlib would be totally impossible in practice because there are so many contributors.

I disagree... these permissive licenses have the precise connotation of "you can copy, tear down this source code, wrap it for commercial use, do whatever you want". Some licenses further say "as long as...". Apache-2 says that as long as the original authors are properly credited, it's okay. No moral infringement given that the original author licensed the source as such.

You can argue that gen AI companies are not complying by training LLMs on sources that are much less permissive as long as it's open source. But I don't see any issue with what Vasily is doing specifically.
@Patrick Massot , what is your specific suggestion?

Patrick Massot said:

For instance changing the licence of Mathlib would be totally impossible in practice because there are so many contributors.

Do you have a different license in mind? Even a GPL-v3 would not prevent Lean Pool. (To the best of my understanding of Lean Pool and GPL v3)

You can still use one of the Apache 2.0 with No AI allowed.
Here a list of NO AI open source licenses to pick on (not sure GitHub recognize them yet):
https://github.com/non-ai-licenses/non-ai-licenses

They only seem to add:

2.1. You shall not use the Covered Software in the creation of an Artificial Intelligence training dataset,
including but not limited to any use that contributes to the training or development of an AI model or algorithm,
unless You obtain explicit written permission from the Contributor to do so.

2.2. You acknowledge that the Covered Software is not intended for use in the creation of an Artificial Intelligence training dataset,
and that the Contributor has no obligation to provide support or assistance for any use that violates this license.

which fully permits Lean Pool.

IMO "open source except for uses I dislike" is not open source
(even if I also dislike those use-cases)
Again this is not a legal issue. It’s a politeness issue.

But that's highly subjective. I, for example, wouldn't care less about whatever people/machines do with the sources I write and release under MIT/Apache licenses, as long as people don't come to me demanding some kind of warranty of correctness/reliability (from which those licenses already exempt me). When I release my sources under permissive licenses, I truly mean it.
Academic ethics and norms of good conduct are not covered by licenses. That doesn’t mean they cease to apply in academic projects that happen to have OSS licenses

Understandable, relatively speaking. I mean, is the body of "academic ethics and norms of good conduct" absolutely agreed upon within the superset of all academic groups?

I'm not claiming that this is a non-issue. I'm claiming that while gray, this will be an endless source of friction with extremely limited actionable items.
I think that just because ethical considerations can be subjective and separate from legal obligations of licensing doesn't mean we shouldn't (in a respectful fashion) discuss them.

@Patrick Massot I would like to stick up for @Vasily Ilin here. I am surprised by your remark that it is "pure bad faith" and then connecting it to AI.

"Bad faith" requires someone consciously refusing to fulfill some sort of obligation driven by a deceptive or malicious motive. I do not think anyone is being deceived here: they put their repositories online for people to use their Lean code. There is nothing inherently malicious or deceptive about then congregating it into a single source repository where many members of our community can access it.

Furthermore, immediately after stating that it is bad faith, you insinuate that this is due to AI. Putting many Lean repositories into one centralized repository has little in substance to do with generative AI. It could either be a human checking these repositories and bumping them or a robot.

I do agree that people should have their work respected, especially when they are so kind as to post it online for everyone to see and use, and that their own terms should govern that use. However, I think it tends to be poor practice in general to have to guess intent. That is what licenses are for.
@Shreyas Srinivas What do you think the appropriate ethics and norms should be here?
Opt-in process with full consent of all authors involved and a veto for even a single objecting author, and all this preceded by a public consultation on this Zulip for such an initiative.

To be clear, I don't consider the license discussion particularly relevant to my stance, since a license covers the most minimal form of copyright. I can't deny that maybe the problem here is that we academics borrowed licenses from the software world on good-faith assumptions.

The MIT License states the following:

Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of this software and associated documentation files (the "Software"), to deal in the Software without restriction, including without limitation the rights to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell copies of the Software...

Is LeanPool, by definition, not just merging a bunch of repositories together?

I understand that you are arguing for the intent of the authors and not textual meaning of the licenses, but here it seems rather straightforward what people are agreeing to.
In general, it is the onus of the person agreeing to a contract to verify its terms.

I don't have time to engage in this discussion, so I will repeat that the license is of no relevance when other rules are applicable.

In general, it is the onus of the person agreeing to a contract to verify its terms.

Actually no, that depends on the legal system you live in. Here in Germany, I can sign on to the most egregious terms and if they are illegal, the terms are void. Even in common law countries there is more nuance than that to contract enforcement. It doesn't matter what the contract states or that I signed it. This is usually how academic norms work. One isn't excused from them because one is borrowing code from a repository with a permissive license.

Further I am not discussing law. I am discussing politeness.

Patrick Massot said:

I think this argument is pure bad faith. All those licences were created before the genAI disaster and nobody could have imagined this. And now it’s too late for many projects. For instance changing the licence of Mathlib would be totally impossible in practice because there are so many contributors.

While I personally agree that Vasily should not have imported these projects without contacting their authors first, Vasily is clearly acting in good faith here. He is responding to criticisms, removing material when asked, and providing an opt-out mechanism. Making the personal attack on him that he is acting in bad faith in not okay.

Opt-in process with full consent of all authors involved and a veto for even a single objecting author

I've contributed to open source projects (both projects in Lean and in more "traditional" communities) pre-AI and one of my motivations has been a belief that open source is a public good and it's worth volunteering time to contribute to it. I think this is not an uncommon motivation among volunteers.

If some other contributor is able to retroactively put restrictions on what the project could be used for, I would consider that as diminishing the "public good" aspect of the project and not "in the spirit" of open source. It's not really polite to me.

The bad faith remark was about a very specific part of the discussion: it was commenting the claim that because people used an open source licence they should be happy their work is used to participate in the genAI apocalypse. Nobody can argue in good faith that anyone could have imagined this when Mathlib for instance chose the Apache licence.
I think you are putting words in Vasily's mouth and then saying that those "words" were spoken in bad faith. I don't think that is appropriate.

Li Xuanji said:

If some other contributor is able to retroactively put restrictions on what the project could be used for, I would consider that as diminishing the "public good" aspect of the project and not "in the spirit" of open source. It's not really polite to me.

I disagree. There can be open source licenses that respect academic norms to some extent and still be consistent with open source principles. See example : https://opensource.org/license/AFL-3.0

Exclusions From License Grant. Neither the names of Licensor, nor the names of any contributors to the Original Work, nor any of their trademarks or service marks, may be used to endorse or promote products derived from this Original Work without express prior permission of the Licensor. Except as expressly stated herein, nothing in this License grants any license to Licensor’s trademarks, copyrights, patents, trade secrets or any other intellectual property.

Working "in the spirit" of open source is not in contradiction with requiring "express prior permission" from authors, even according to the OSI.

Kim Morrison said:

I think you are putting words in Vasily's mouth and then saying that those "words" were spoken in bad faith. I don't think that is appropriate.

I'd like to try phrasing my own personal opinion in a way that does not put words in anyone's mouth or constitute a personal attack. I would say that the following are simultaneously true:

  • an aggregation of projects like Lean Pool, regardless of intended use, is permitted under their OSS licences
  • there are additional social/ethical considerations beyond the legal framework of licensing
  • these are not retroactive or binding: these are inherently subjective and you are free to ignore them
  • I would not have constructed Lean Pool without contacting authors, but Vasily also had no obligation to do so and has responded to this thread beyond their legal obligation

Some care has to be taken with wording, but I do not think that @Patrick Massot intended any personal attack. We should be able to sternly but respectfully push back against arguments that imply that permissive OSS licensing means that we have to be supportive of any legally permitted use case, especially when AI has significantly changed this landscape beneath our feet.

Patrick Massot dijo:

I think this argument is pure bad faith. All those licences were created before the genAI disaster and nobody could have imagined this. And now it’s too late for many projects. For instance changing the licence of Mathlib would be totally impossible in practice because there are so many contributors.

There have been big evil companies using open source long before AI was a thing, and there will continue to be big evil companies long after AI is gone. If you want full legal control over who uses your code and how, then you should not contribute to open source.

This sounds like a difference between two cultures around sharing and reusing work: "open source software" and "academic mathematics" (if that name isn't quite right, what would you call it?)

Like some others, I also don't see how any of this is related to AI use or even the recent changes to the ecosystem due to AI. Is that perhaps a crucial point to understand here?

It has been said that "Lean Pool is not OK" follows from "academic ethics and good conduct". As a physics PhD student, my understanding and interpretation of these (admittedly limited due to not being an experienced academic and unlikely to ever become one) do not lead me to the same conclusion. I'm wondering how to better understand those norms. Is it something one can only learn by being an academic? Maybe these things are written down somewhere? Given that Lean is very much at the intersection of math and open source, we should make it easy for anyone interested to understand both cultures and their norms, including having sources to learn about them.

As someone admittedly also not yet really familiar with OSS social norms, my zeroth-order approximation is that licenses communicate intent of creators and contributors and what is expected from users not only legally but also socially. Licenses are also usually enforced by social norms and much more rarely by legal means.

What would be the zeroth-order summary of the norms that make Lean Pool not OK? To better understand the perspective of those who think Lean Pool is not OK, some questions, where (if anyone is willing to comment on them) I'm especially interested in the reasoning behind the answer:

  • Is using Lean projects with OSS licenses as a dependency (putting a link in the lakefile, which downloads, compiles and uses the code) OK? (I assume yes since most projects do this.) Would LeanPool be OK if it was instead just putting all the links in the lakefile and importing all of them? (I personally don't see a big difference here)
  • Is forking projects and making minor changes in a branch with no intention to make PRs to the main repository OK? E.g., to make it work better as a dependency for some other project one has? Would LeanPool be OK if there was a fork of each project (to make them compatible and work with the same toolchain etc.) and the main repository just imported everything?
  • Is forking and taking a project in a different direction OK? E.g., is it OK to fork Mathlib and work on removing the choice axiom?

As far as I understand, all of these would be consistent with OSS social norms if one checked that nothing in the repository indicates expectations beyond the license (e.g. a note like "please never feed this into an AI", regardless of whether it's legally meaningful).

As I understand it, some open-source projects have a development culture that hinges on community building and consensus rather than simply working code. In those situations, forking is only acceptable when there are irreconcilable differences in long term goals, because it means a potential split in the community.
If Lean Pool acts as a snapshot-and-minimal-update library, then it is not quite as bad as it could be if it were soliciting active development of the snapshotted projects, since in the former case, it is unlikely to lead to a split in the community around an active project.

From the academic side, if someone shoehorned themselves into an ongoing project, and tried to build off independently, then it is disrespectful of authorship precedence and of the expectations of respectful behaviour towards researchers. It is the equivalent of listening to a preliminary talk on the work in a workshop and then rushing in a paper before the authors do it.

Even a GPL-v3 would not prevent Lean Pool

@Henrik Böving , can you please explain why you would like to "prevent Lean Pool"? If you don't want to talk in public, feel free to send me a DM. I want to understand how the community feels.

I don't have a particular feeling towards this but it seemed to me that some people in this stream thought that with a different license it would've been possible to make it impossible for Lean Pool to use a project in this way and I just wanted to point out that this is not the case for any popular open source license at the moment.

Opt-in process with full consent of all authors involved and a veto for even a single objecting author

This is exactly what the current process is already. The opt-in is via open licenses (MIT, Apache-2). And I have repeatedly said that I will remove any project that an author of the project would like removed. So far not a single project author has asked me to remove any of their projects.
I think "opt-in" in that message refers to "please add this repo to Lean Pool", as the discussion that followed clarified

it is unlikely to lead to a split in the community around an active project.

@Scott Carnahan , this is an important point. I intentionally did not import active projects in Lean Pool. My heuristic is that the last commit to main was over 2 months ago and the Lean version is v4.28 or lower. And I am happy to remove any project when an author asks, so if a project becomes active again, it can be removed from Lean Pool.

If I may, I would like to pose an open-ended question to the community, which is separate from the issue of licenses (which unfortunately has dominated the discussion so far).

It is clear that mathlib cannot stay the only dependency for new projects - this is just too restrictive. However, the monorepo design of mathlib is incredibly convenient. My question, which inspired Lean Pool, is

How can the Lean community build an open-source monorepo library that scales faster than mathlib, while ensuring as much of the quality as possible?

I am 90% sure that AI companies have their own internal versions of Lean Pool or forks of mathlib. It would be a shame if one of them released theirs, which is 10x or 100x larger than mathlib and contains e.g. most of arXiv formalized or e.g. the top 10,000 most cited papers formalized, and made it a paid service for academics to depend on it or to interact with an agent that has access to it. I anticipate that this will happen in late 2026 or early 2027, so we have maybe 5 months to answer the above question. Lean Pool is my answer.

@Vasily Ilin : since I am the one who wrote opt-in, let me clarify. I mean that you need to explicitly explain what you are doing to each author of every single respository, wait for their response as long as it takes, and explicitly obtain their consent for each use. Licenses are not “opt-in”. I am also not talking about whatever else the software industry or OSS world pleases to call standards for defining the words “opt-in”. I am talking about the kind of courtesy one expects in academic work.

But all this discussion, and especially the divergence Adomas points out seems to indicate that we need to start using an explicitly academic license that encodes these assumptions. We can’t rely on norms and good faith assumptions that we take for granted in academia to hold outside academia. If this breaks the spirit of open source or hinders AI companies, personally I am gladly willing to accept that as a necessary consequence of fostering healthy respect for each other’s effort and right to have their work used, extended, and credited appropriately. Further, imo anything that hinders AI is a huge positive.

We can't rely on norms and good faith assumptions pretty much anywhere, not even in academia :shrug:

But I'm not a defeatist. I think a targeted license is a real need these days. Though it is not guaranteed to prevent LLM-driven companies from devouring the work you open source. That's a different fight. And it's not what Vasily did... he's not training models behind anyone's back, as far as I'm concerned.

Want to fight the momentum of such AI companies? I stand nowhere on that fight. But my impression is that the Lean FRO itself is aligned with their goals. Important remark: it's my personal view.

My concern is that most of the deterministic safeguards discussed so far seem to be ex post checks, such as CI, linters, and compilation. These are useful, but they do not address the non-deterministic part of the process, how the LLM reviewer itself reaches a moderation or acceptance decision.

What I would suggest to create common ground is to introduce a reasoning graph as an intermediate layer between the LLM reviewer and the final Lean code, especially if the LLM reviewer plays a significant gatekeeping role beyond Lean’s formal checking.

A reasoning graph could help bridge the different perspectives here. It would impose a structured representation of the review process as trusted statements, candidate proofs, dependencies, subgoals, accepted or rejected transformations, and verification steps. Ideally, this would be grounded in Comparator style validation like checking whether a proposed proof actually proves the intended statement, instead of relying only on a textual LLM review.

This would make the process more auditable and controllable, rather than leaving the agentic and LLM-review parts mostly opaque.

And regarding open-source/MIT licensing, if some authors want to restrict the intended openness of their work to human use only, they should make that explicit in the repository. But this would also mean changing the definition of "open source", since open-source licensing traditionally does not restrict who or what can reuse the code.

I am very happy with the open nature of Mathlib and the surrounding ecosystem. If we want to learn lessons from academia, it would rather be how not to organize sharing work with others. It's been a relief to do maths in an OSS context instead of the crazy copyright system that the academic maths community can't seem to escape.

I am not speaking for mathlib. Two of my repositories were included in this lean pool. Since it is compared to arxiv, I would like to point out that one has to actively submit papers to arxiv first. Arxiv doesn’t assume that we opt-in because we had some license attached to an online manuscript.

Public domain. No rights reserved. This work may be translated or copied in whole or in part with-
out the written permission of the author. Use in connection with any form of information storage
and retrieval, electronic adaptation, computer software, or by similar or dissimilar methodology
now known or hereafter developed is explicitly encouraged.

Source: https://math.commelin.net/files/thesis.pdf

:shrug:

@Johan Commelin : just a question that is analogous to what is happening here. If someone took your thesis, added two chapters of their own (possibly sloppy and incorrect with hallucinated references), and appended their name to the authors field, and then submitted it to arxiv, would you approve of this? Because your quoted statement would permit this.

I am of course making this analogy keeping in mind arxiv’s recent policy change about authors of slop submissions.
Yes, if they want to do that. Joke's on them.

The reason I am referring to that policy is because it entails a ban on all listed authors from submitting anything to arxiv for a year and then a lifelong condition that all submitted work is already published. Note that currently arxiv doesn’t ask explicit permission from each listed author before accepting a submission (another case of lax implementation of academic standards), but the ban applies to all the authors.

What license the original work is under seems unrelated there. If someone takes a thesis which does not allow public re-use and slops it up and uploads it the same bad outcome occurs in this hypothetical.
(There's no way arxiv would enforce a ban on an author who didn't participate in actually uploading or consenting to upload, one would have to think.)

Vasily Ilin said:

How can the Lean community build an open-source monorepo library that scales faster than mathlib, while ensuring as much of the quality as possible?

I think the main part of "quality" in mathlib is digestion, in Tao's terms, which simply taking lots of separate projects and putting them together in a monorepo does not achieve.

  1. Improve mathlib review times. I don't know how to do this, but subjectively it feels like they were a lot better in the Lean 3 era; that back then (when there were maybe a tenth as many open PRs as there are now in mathlib4) I could open several PRs with the work done at a weekend and expect that by the next weekend most of them (and a few layers of dependent PRs on top of them) would be merged into mathlib ready to use as a basis for the next weekend's work (and certainly that replies to a reviewer's comments wouldn't wait weeks or months for further progress in the conversation).
  2. Make better use of the mathlib archive, which is something between mathlib and Lean Pool - I feel it should be a natural location for lots of completed formalizations that aren't being used as a basis for further work. The discussion around licenses is not motivated by whether it stops bad actors or not, but whether it gives authors some tools to protect their work from unintended exploitation or seek remedy after the fact. It is relevant here because using the Apache license or MIT license has been interpreted as “opt-in” for lean pool. Ultimately all I am opining is that “opt-in” needs to be explicit and at least I did not intentionally opt in to lean pool. Consider this alternative universe:

  1. @Vasily Ilin and collaborators create a fork of your repo to LeanPool/yourRepo
  2. They do whatever they thing necessary to bump it to the latest lean version
  3. They add some boilerplate to the readme to explain how this relates to the original project
  4. They git submodule add LeanPool/yourRepo to LeanPool/Pool
  5. They repeat steps 1-4 for many other projects
  6. They make a Zulip announcement just like this one

The end result is effectively the same; a repo that you can git clone to get compatible versions of all the packages.

For those who find LeanPool objectionable, is this strategy equally objectionable from an ownership point of view? If so, which step is the problematic one? If not, what makes this meaningfully different from LeanPool's current approach?
(I discussed this approach with @Vasily Ilin during the hackathon, but we concluded it would be a lot of extra infra work that wouldn't fit within the hackathon timelines)

Improve mathlib review times.

Certainly it would be great if mathlib review times could be improved. Indeed, my understanding is that the mathlib initiative was founded with this as one of its main initial purposes. But it seems likely to me that whatever marginal improvements we can make to the review system to make it go faster, mathlib will still be fundamentally bottlenecked by the amount of human review time available (also I would posit that one of the reasons that it is hard to solve the problem of long mathlib review times is that the shorter review times become, the more attractive submitting PRs to mathlib becomes).

So I am led to think that even though AI maintained lean libraries will not be as high in quality as mathlib, they still might be the best way of getting libraries of marginal quality that work.
